assessment.nobel_worthiness: Dynamical mean-field theory is the first controlled non-perturbative framework that treats local correlations and band structure on equal footing. It underlies modern understanding of the Mott transition and, combined with electronic-structure methods (DFT+DMFT), gives quantitative access to correlated materials such as transition-metal oxides, f-electron systems and iron-based compounds. Its originality is high (the infinite-dimension limit) and its influence on computational condensed-matter physics is broad and lasting.
assessment.attribution: The infinite-dimensional limit goes back to Metzner and Vollhardt, with the mapping to an impurity problem and the Mott-transition solution by Georges and Kotliar and collaborators. The three supplied names cover the core conceptual and methodological steps reasonably, but Metzner, Müller-Hartmann and Jarrell-type solver contributions are not in the supplied credit, so the configuration is defensible rather than complete.
assessment.maturity: Developed from 1989 to the mid 1990s and tested for three decades against experiment and other methods; extensions (cluster DMFT, DFT+DMFT) are widely used. Recognition is timely and the interpretation is stable. Remaining limits concern finite-dimension corrections, not the validity of the core idea.
uncertainties: Whether the credit supplied omits decisive contributors such as Metzner and Müller-Hartmann.
Prize-worthy as a theoretical method; the committee may weigh whether discovery-oriented work should take precedence.
Unverified from memory: the exact chronology of priority between the groups.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Room-temperature tunnel magnetoresistance in magnetic tunnel junctions, followed by giant TMR in MgO-based junctions, underlies read heads and magnetic random-access memory. It is a clear case of spin-dependent tunnelling in magnetic multilayers with exceptional technological reach, and it follows naturally from the 2007 prize on giant magnetoresistance. Understanding of the coherent-tunnelling mechanism in crystalline MgO is a strong scientific component.
assessment.attribution: Miyazaki and Moodera independently reported room-temperature TMR in 1995; Parkin and Yuasa/Djayaprawira groups demonstrated giant TMR with MgO in 2004. The theoretical prediction for Fe/MgO/Fe (Butler, Mathon) is not in the supplied credit, and the Yuasa and Djayaprawira contributions are also absent, so the three-person configuration is fair but leaves real attribution problems.
assessment.maturity: Thirty years of confirmation and deployment in hard drives and MRAM; very mature and independent. Timing is somewhat late rather than premature, but a prize remains appropriate.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2007 GMR prize may be viewed as incremental.
The MgO-based giant TMR credit involves people not in the supplied list.
Exact priority details recalled from memory and not verified.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The prediction of the quantum spin Hall effect and Z2 topological insulators, and its experimental realisation in HgTe quantum wells, opened a whole field of topological band theory and protected edge and surface states. The conceptual originality is very high, the theory is clean, and the experiment gave a decisive confirmation. Electronic-structure calculations of band inversion played a key role in guiding materials choices, which I find convincing.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele introduced the Z2 classification and the quantum spin Hall idea; Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang proposed the HgTe route, and Molenkamp's group observed it. Hasan contributed the first 3D topological insulator observations by ARPES, while Fu and Moore and others also contributed theoretically. The supplied names allow a fair three-person prize but with visible exclusions.
assessment.maturity: Fifteen to twenty years of independent confirmation across many materials; the interpretation is stable and the field is mature. Timing is appropriate.
uncertainties: Competing claims by Bernevig, Zhang, Fu, Hasan complicate allocation.
Potential concern that topological phases are partially covered by the 2016 prize.
Details of priority recalled from memory.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The prediction of flat bands at the magic angle in twisted bilayer graphene and the observation of correlated insulating and superconducting states created moiré quantum matter, a tunable platform for strongly correlated physics. It is an unusually clean link between a simple electronic-structure calculation and a surprising experimental outcome, and graphene-based systems changed expectations for two-dimensional materials.
assessment.attribution: Bistritzer and MacDonald made the continuum-model prediction in 2011 and Jarillo-Herrero's group observed the correlated and superconducting states in 2018. Cao as first author and other experimental groups share the credit, but the three supplied names make a clean theory-plus-experiment configuration.
assessment.maturity: Confirmed independently by multiple groups and reproduced over several years, with a broad expansion to other moiré systems. Some microscopic questions about the superconductivity are still open, so recognition could be seen as slightly early, but the core discovery is solid.
uncertainties: Mechanism of superconductivity remains unsettled.
Sample-dependence and reproducibility of some phases.
Credit for the young first author and other theory groups not included.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Spherical-aberration correction in transmission electron microscopy broke a decades-old limit and brought routine sub-angstrom imaging of atoms and defects, with large consequences for materials science, interfaces, catalysts and two-dimensional materials. This is an instrument-based invention with clear, lasting scientific influence, and it is the kind of enabling capability that I see supporting every part of materials theory by delivering atomic-scale validation.
assessment.attribution: Rose provided the theoretical design of the corrector, Haider and Urban built and demonstrated it. The credited names map well onto the decisive roles and offer a clean three-person configuration. Other contributors such as Krivanek and colleagues for the STEM corrector are not in the credit.
assessment.maturity: Developed in the 1990s and now commercial and routine worldwide; very mature. Timely given the prize tradition for instruments (electron microscope 1986).
uncertainties: Parallel STEM-corrector work by Krivanek and others may require allocation.
Whether the committee sees this as physics versus instrumentation.
Prior awards (Wolf Prize) recalled from memory.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Discovery of high-temperature superconductivity in iron pnictides in 2008 opened the second family of high-Tc superconductors, with multiband and magnetism-linked pairing. The first-principles community quickly contributed Fermi-surface and spin-fluctuation analyses. The scientific importance is high, though the mechanism is still debated.
assessment.attribution: Kamihara and Hosono reported LaFeAsO(1-x)Fx with Tc about 26 K, with Hosono as the clear senior leader. The supplied credit is compact and plausible, with a two-person prize. Follow-up groups in China that raised Tc to 55 K are not included.
assessment.maturity: Well confirmed and extensively replicated, but the pairing mechanism has not converged and no technology followed at scale; recognition would be on discovery alone, which is acceptable but slightly less decisive.
uncertainties: Pairing mechanism unresolved.
Chinese groups' rapid Tc enhancements and their credit.
Hosono's earlier work on the material class recalled from memory.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Ultracold atoms in optical lattices implement Hubbard-type models with tunable parameters, giving quantum simulators of correlated matter, the superfluid to Mott-insulator transition and now fermionic Hubbard physics with single-site resolution. The link to the correlated-electron problems that I study theoretically is direct, and the field is now a major source of benchmark data.
assessment.attribution: Jaksch, Zoller and collaborators proposed the Bose-Hubbard realisation; Greiner, Bloch and Hänsch observed the Mott transition; Esslinger and Greiner contributed fermionic and microscope work. The supplied list has five names, so a three-person selection necessarily leaves out important contributors, and Cirac and Zoller are also the subject of another ballot entry.
assessment.maturity: Mature in bosonic experiments; fermionic Hubbard simulation is advancing but not yet decisive for open questions about high-Tc physics.
uncertainties: Limited experimental credit space with five credited names.
Overlap with a separate Cirac-Zoller candidate.
Open question of whether quantum simulation has solved an unsolved problem.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Circuit quantum electrodynamics provided the architecture for strong coupling of superconducting qubits to microwave resonators, enabling readout, control and scalable quantum processors. It is important for quantum technology and for fundamental quantum optics in a solid-state setting.
assessment.attribution: Blais, Huang, Wallraff, Girvin and Schoelkopf wrote the 2004 proposal and demonstration; Girvin is not among the supplied names, which makes the allocation incomplete. The three supplied names are a reasonable subset.
assessment.maturity: Mature in experiments with more than twenty years of use, but the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in superconducting circuits has just recognised nearby work, so a follow-up now may be seen as premature or overlapping.
uncertainties: Proximity to the 2025 prize.
Girvin and Devoret-related credit overlaps not in the supplied names.
Technology impact is still evolving.
